title: Compliance for finance, trading and gambling offers
summary: How law, advertiser licences, platform authorization and network rules stack for trading, gambling and loan offers, and how to check each one in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, South Africa, Cameroon and beyond. You finish with honest creatives, a compliance file and an exact go/no-go gate, so you never launch a regulated campaign you cannot defend. Education, not legal advice.

lessons.title: How regulation and platform policy stack
objectives: By the end you can name the four layers of rules that apply to every regulated campaign.
You can explain why passing one layer never means you passed the others.
You can verify an advertiser's licence on a regulator's official register.
You can apply a simple go/no-go rule: every layer must be a clear yes.

steps.h: Why this is the one module you cannot fail
steps.p: Trading, gambling and loan offers pay well because they are risky for the people who use them. That is why they are regulated. A mistake here does not only waste ad spend. It can get your ad account banned, your payouts withheld and, in some countries, expose you to fines or criminal charges.
steps.more: Most modules teach you how to earn more. This one teaches you how to keep what you earn. In regulated verticals the rules come from several places at once, and each one can stop your campaign on its own. You do not need to be a lawyer to follow this module. You need to know which questions to ask, where to check the answers and when to say no. Everything here is education, not legal advice. Where we are not certain a rule is current, we say so, and you must check the official source.

d.b: Regulated offers: high payouts, high stakes
d.s: One careless ad can cost the account, the payouts and the business.

steps.h: The four layers every campaign sits inside
steps.p: Picture four filters stacked on top of each other. The law where the user lives decides if the product may be offered. The advertiser's licence proves they are allowed. The platform's authorization decides if the ad may run. The network's rules decide if you get paid. Your ad reaches people only if all four say yes.
steps.more: Read the map from left to right. If the law in Kenya does not allow an unlicensed broker to market there, it does not matter that Meta approved your ad. If Meta has not authorized gambling ads for your account, it does not matter that the casino holds a licence. If the network bans a certain type of traffic, your conversions can be rejected even when everything else is legal. Each layer is a separate question with a separate answer, and you must collect all four answers before you spend.

steps.p: Each layer has a different owner and asks a different question. Learn the question each one asks, because that tells you who to ask and what proof to collect.
d: Law|Can this product be offered and advertised to people in this country?
Licence|Is this advertiser authorised by the regulator for this exact country?
Platform|Has the ad platform given permission for this category and account?
Network|Do the offer terms allow this traffic source, geo and message?

Licence asks, is this advertiser authorised by the regulator for this exact country? Platform asks, has the ad platform given permission for this category and account? And network asks, do the offer terms allow this traffic source, geo and message? Learn the question each one asks, because it tells you who to ask and what proof to collect.

steps.h: Who sets each layer and what breaking it costs
steps.p: A rough guide. The cost of breaking a layer depends on the country, the platform and your contract, so treat this as a map of risk, not a list of exact penalties.
steps.more: Notice that the most expensive consequences come from the layers you cannot see in Ads Manager. A rejected ad is visible and cheap. A regulator's order or a network clawback can arrive weeks later, after you have spent and reinvested. That delay is why you check everything before launch, not after.

steps.say: This table is a rough guide to who sets each layer and what breaking it can cost. Law is set by government and regulators, and breaking it can mean fines, orders or possible charges. Licence is set by the regulator, and without it the offer is illegal there. Platform rules from Meta, TikTok or Google can get ads rejected and accounts restricted. Network rules can mean rejected leads and withheld payouts. Notice the most expensive consequences come from layers you can't see in Ads Manager, and they can arrive weeks later. steps.p: When two layers disagree, follow the stricter one. If local law says 18 and the advertiser's terms say 21, use 21. If the platform allows a claim but the regulator forbids it, do not make it. You never get to pick the softer rule because it suits your campaign.

steps.p: Many brokers and betting brands you promote in Africa are licensed in other countries too. These are common examples. A licence in one of these places does not by itself permit marketing in Nigeria, Kenya or anywhere else.

steps.h: How to verify a licence on an official register
steps.p: Never trust a licence number on a sales page alone. Check it yourself on the regulator's own site. This takes ten minutes and protects weeks of spend. Screens here are illustrative mock-ups; every register looks different.

steps.title: Go to the regulator yourself
steps.text: Type the regulator's address or find it via a search you trust. Do not click the link on the offer page; fake registers exist.

blocks.value: Official site of the financial regulator

steps.title: Search the firm
steps.text: Search by the legal company name and the licence number the advertiser gave you, not only the brand name.

steps.title: Check status and scope
steps.text: Status should be current or authorised. Check what the firm is permitted to do, for example dealing in CFDs or offering consumer credit.

steps.title: Match the website
steps.text: The register should list the same website domain your offer sends users to. A different domain is a warning sign of a clone.

steps.title: Save the proof
steps.text: Take a screenshot showing the date, the URL and the status. File it in your compliance folder from lesson 6.

steps.say: Never trust a licence number on a sales page alone. Check it yourself. Tap Next to follow each step. First, go to the regulator's site yourself, by typing the address or using a search you trust. Don't click the link on the offer page, because fake registers exist. Second, search by the legal company name and the licence number, not just the brand. Third, check the status is current or authorised, and what the firm is permitted to do. Fourth, make sure the register lists the same website domain your offer uses. Fifth, save a dated screenshot to your compliance folder. These screens are illustrative mock-ups.

steps.p: A clone firm copies the name, licence number and look of a real licensed company, then uses its own website to take people's money. Regulators publish warning lists about clones and unlicensed firms. If the domain on the register does not match the offer, stop and ask the network in writing.

As the warning says, if the licence number matches but the website doesn't, treat it as a clone until proven otherwise.

steps.h: The order of checks before you build anything
steps.p: Do the checks in this order, because each one can end the plan and later checks are wasted if an earlier one fails. Building creatives first and checking the law last is the most expensive way round.
d: Law allows it in this geo
Advertiser licensed for this geo
Platform authorization granted
Network terms allow your source
Then build ads and landers
steps.say: Follow this flow, in order, before you build anything. First, the law allows it in this geo. Second, the advertiser is licensed for this geo. Third, platform authorization is granted. Fourth, the network terms allow your source. Only then, build ads and landers. Why this order? Because each check can end the plan, and later checks are wasted if an earlier one fails. Building creatives first and checking the law last is the most expensive way round.

steps.p: Example. You run a casino offer into a country where online casino is not permitted. Ads get approved, sign-ups come in, and the network reviews the geo at month end. Every figure is illustrative, not a statistic.
steps.more: Example maths: 10 days at $40 is $400. Twelve FTDs at $50 would have paid $600, so you expected a $200 profit. Instead the network rejects everything because the brand cannot legally accept players from that geo, so you lose the $400 you spent and never see the $600. The gap between plan and reality is $1,000, and that is before you count the risk to your ad account and to your relationship with the network. Ten minutes on a register and one written question to the network would have prevented all of it.

steps.h: Why gambling is the strictest vertical
steps.p: Gambling can cause real harm: debt, addiction and family breakdown. Regulators and platforms respond with the tightest rules in advertising. A single ad that appeals to children or promises easy money can end your account and, in some countries, break the law.
steps.more: This lesson covers sports betting, online casino, lotteries and other games where people stake money to win money. Some sweepstakes and skill games can fall under gambling rules too, depending on the platform and country. If you are not sure whether your offer counts as gambling, assume it does until the platform's current policy and the local law say otherwise.

d.b: Gambling ads are judged on harm
d.s: Every rule exists because someone was hurt.

Online casino, like slots, roulette and live dealer games. Lotteries, including some private ones. Skill games for money, like fantasy, poker and paid tournaments. And some sweepstakes where entry costs money.

steps.h: 18+ is the floor, and sometimes higher
steps.p: Gambling is adults only. In most of our core markets the legal age is 18. Some places set it higher; many US states, for example, set 21 for casino gambling. Your targeting, creatives and landers must all respect the highest age that applies.
steps.more: Age rules reach further than targeting. In the UK, for example, the advertising codes at the time of writing say people shown in a significant role in gambling ads must not be, or seem to be, under 25, and ads must not strongly appeal to under-18s. Even outside the UK this is a sensible standard: no school uniforms, cartoon characters, youth slang aimed at teenagers or young-looking actors. Age targeting in Ads Manager uses the age people state on their profile, which is not perfect, so your creative must also not attract children.

steps.p: Example. A bonus says "100% up to KSh 5,000" with 10x wagering on the bonus. A user deposits KSh 1,000 and gets KSh 1,000 bonus. Before they can withdraw bonus winnings they must place KSh 10,000 in bets. Your ad must not hide that.
steps.more: Example maths: bonus KSh 1,000 multiplied by a 10x wagering requirement equals KSh 10,000 of bets. Some brands apply wagering to deposit plus bonus, which would double it to KSh 20,000; read the real terms. An ad that says "Get KSh 1,000 free" without the wagering is misleading in many places and drives users who feel tricked, complain and churn. Show the key terms near the offer, such as "18+. Min deposit KSh 100. 10x wagering. T&Cs apply.", and link the full terms on the lander.

steps.h: Worked example: where the percentage comes from
steps.p: Example only. The percentage is the share of the provider's retail client accounts that lost money over a recent period. You do not calculate it yourself; you use the figure the broker publishes. This shows the maths so you understand what it means.

Use the broker's current figure, put it where users will read it, and update creatives when it changes.

steps.h: Why loan ads can hurt people
steps.p: A loan ad reaches people who often need money now. Hidden fees, rolling debt and aggressive collection can turn a small loan into a crisis. Regulators in our core markets have acted against lenders and apps over these harms, so lending ads are watched closely.
steps.more: This lesson covers loans, credit cards, buy now pay later, insurance, savings and banking lead generation. Each has its own licence type and disclosure rules. Lending has the clearest harms, so it gets the most attention here. Regulators in Nigeria and Kenya, for example, have acted against digital lenders over practices such as shaming borrowers by contacting people in their phone book; this matters to you because the apps you promote reflect on your account and your name.

d.s: Show the full cost, and never target desperation.

steps.p: Example. A user borrows NGN 50,000 for 30 days and repays NGN 57,500. The fee is NGN 7,500, which is 15% for one month. Over a year that is a much bigger number, which is why many rules require an annualised rate.
steps.more: Example maths: 7,500 divided by 50,000 is 0.15, or 15% for 30 days. Multiply by 365 / 30 (about 12.17) and you get about 182.5% per year as a simple annualised rate. Official APR formulas differ by country and often include compounding and all mandatory fees, which can make the figure higher. Do not calculate the official APR yourself for an ad; ask the lender for the figure and the representative example their regulator requires, and show it as given.

steps.h: Why the rewrite pays for itself

d.b: Honest copy is copy that lasts

steps.say: When a platform reviews your account, a network audits your traffic, or a regulator asks a question, the only thing that helps is proof. A short, organised file shows what you checked, when, and on whose advice. Without it, you're asking people to trust your memory. If it's not written down, it didn't happen. Proof turns a dispute into a conversation.

steps.h: What to keep for every regulated offer
steps.p: Collect these before launch and update them whenever anything changes. Most are screenshots, emails or PDFs that take a few minutes each to save, and together they show exactly what you checked and when.
d: Licence proofs|Dated register screenshots per geo
Platform authorizations|Approval emails, permission screens
Network terms|Offer terms and every written answer
Approved copy|Final ads, landers and warnings used
Consent logs|What each lead agreed to, when, with what text
Advice|Notes from lawyers or advisers, dated
steps.say: Look at these six cards. For every regulated offer, keep licence proofs, meaning dated register screenshots per geo. Platform authorizations, like approval emails and permission screens. Network terms, with the offer terms and every written answer. Approved copy, the final ads, landers and warnings used. Consent logs, what each lead agreed to, when, and with what text. And advice, dated notes from lawyers or advisers. Collect these before launch, and update them whenever anything changes.

steps.p: One folder per offer and geo keeps everything findable, even months later or when a teammate needs it. Use dates in file names so the newest proof is obvious and older versions stay as history.

steps.h: What one consent record looks like
steps.p: For every lead, store enough to prove what the person agreed to, when and through which form. Link the record to the exact version of the consent text shown, because wording changes over time.
steps.more: Keep consent records secure, limit who can see them and set a deletion date. How long you must keep records depends on the law and your contracts, so ask your adviser; do not keep personal data longer than you need. If a person asks what you hold or asks you to delete it, the record tells you exactly where their data went, which many data protection laws require you to answer.

d.note: Example record. Store securely and only as long as you need it.

That means a lead reference, the time, the source form, the version of the consent text shown, which consents they gave, and who the data was shared with. Linking to the exact text version matters because wording changes over time. Keep these records secure, limit who sees them, and don't keep personal data longer than you need. Ask your adviser how long to keep them.

steps.p: Use this exact gate for every new regulated campaign, geo or major creative change. Every line must be a yes with a file in the folder. One no or one unknown means no launch. This is a starting gate; adapt it with your adviser.
d: 1. Law: product may be offered and advertised in this geo, source filed
2. Licence: entity verified on official register for this geo, dated screenshot
3. Platform: authorization or special category in place where required
4. Network: source, geo, copy and age written and filed
5. Copy: passes creative checklist; warnings visible on mobile
6. Data: privacy policy live, consent text versioned, records stored
steps.say: Here's the pre-launch go or no-go gate. Use it for every new regulated campaign, geo or major creative change. One: law, the product may be offered and advertised in this geo, with a source filed. Two: licence, the entity verified on the official register, with a dated screenshot. Three: platform, authorization or special category in place where required. Four: network, source, geo, copy and age in writing. Five: copy passes the checklist, with warnings visible on mobile. Six: data, privacy policy live, consent text versioned, records stored. One no or one unknown means no launch.

steps.h: When a network asks for non-compliant copy
steps.p: Networks and managers sometimes push copy that converts but breaks rules. Your reply should be polite, written and firm, and it should offer a compliant alternative.

messages.text: Top affiliates run "guaranteed 300% returns". Use it and we raise your payout.
I cannot run guaranteed return claims. They break platform policy and local rules.
I can run demo-account and education angles with the risk warning. Can you confirm that copy in writing?
OK, send it over for approval.

steps.say: Networks and managers sometimes push copy that converts but breaks rules. In this chat, notice how it's handled. The manager says top affiliates run guaranteed three hundred percent returns, and offers a higher payout. You reply that you can't run guaranteed return claims, because they break platform policy and local rules. Then you offer demo account and education angles with the risk warning, and ask for written confirmation. Your reply should be polite, written and firm, and offer a compliant alternative.

steps.h: What to do when asked to break the rules
steps.p: Follow the same steps every time, so the decision is never made under pressure or for a higher payout. Writing it down also protects you if the network later claims you ran the copy on your own.
d: Do not run it
Reply in writing with the reason
Offer a compliant alternative
Escalate if they insist
Walk away if they still insist
File the whole exchange
steps.say: Follow the same steps every time you're asked to break the rules. Don't run it. Reply in writing with the reason. Offer a compliant alternative. Escalate if they insist. Walk away if they still insist. And file the whole exchange. Doing it the same way every time means the decision is never made under pressure, or for a higher payout. Writing it down also protects you if the network later claims you ran the copy on your own.

steps.p: Most buyers do some checking. The problem is usually that the proof is scattered, undated or missing on the day it is needed, so the checking cannot be shown to anyone.

steps.h: Worked example: the cost of keeping a file
steps.p: Example. A file takes about 20 minutes per campaign to set up. With 10 new campaigns a month that is 200 minutes, about 3.3 hours. Compare that with one disputed month of payouts.
steps.more: Example maths: 20 minutes x 10 campaigns = 200 minutes, and 200 divided by 60 is about 3.3 hours. If a network disputes $2,000 of payouts and claims your geo or copy broke the terms, the file is what lets you show the written approval and the copy you actually ran. Without it, the network's word usually wins. The figures are illustrative; your own time and payouts will differ.

steps.p: Rejections, restrictions and complaints happen even to careful buyers. Respond calmly, with facts from your file and through the official process. Never open new accounts to get around a restriction.
d: Ad rejected|Read reason, fix cause, note it in the file
Account restricted|Appeal through the official process with your proof
Network clawback|Send your written approvals and copy history
User complaint|Pause, review, respond honestly, record the outcome
Regulator contact|Stop and speak to a qualified lawyer first
steps.say: Rejections, restrictions and complaints happen even to careful buyers. Here's how to respond. Ad rejected: read the reason, fix the cause, note it in the file. Account restricted: appeal through the official process with your proof. Network clawback: send your written approvals and copy history. User complaint: pause, review, respond honestly, record the outcome. Regulator contact: stop, and speak to a qualified lawyer first. Respond calmly, with facts, and never open new accounts to get around a restriction.

Recheck before any budget increase above 2x
Update risk warnings when the broker's figure changes
Reread platform policy pages for your verticals

Recheck before any budget increase above two times. Update risk warnings when the broker's figure changes. Reread platform policy pages for your verticals. And delete personal data past its retention date. Licences get suspended, warnings change and policies are updated, so a check that was true at launch may not be true a month later.

quiz.q: Your gate shows 5 of 6 lines as yes; the platform authorization is still pending. What is the status?
options: GO at half budget
GO, five is enough
NO-GO until authorization is granted
GO on a different platform without checking
quiz.why: Any no or unknown line means no launch. The gate only works if it is applied exactly.

quiz.q: A manager approved your geo on a voice call. What do you do?
options: Ask them to confirm it in writing and file the reply
Nothing, a call is enough
Record the call without telling them
Launch and ask later
quiz.why: A written confirmation is proof you can file. Memories of calls do not help in a dispute.

quiz.q: A network offers a higher payout if you use "guaranteed returns" copy. What is the right first reply?
options: Accept but soften it to "almost guaranteed"
Run it on one ad set only
Ignore the message
Decline in writing and offer compliant copy
quiz.why: Do not run it, explain why in writing and propose an alternative. File the exchange.

quiz.q: 20 minutes per campaign, 12 campaigns a month. How long is the filing?
options: 2 hours
4 hours
3 hours
6 hours
quiz.why: 20 x 12 = 240 minutes, which is 4 hours. Small compared with one payout dispute you cannot prove.

quiz.q: When should you recheck a licence on the register?
options: Only at first launch
Only when the network asks
Monthly and before scaling
Once a year
quiz.why: Licences can be suspended or changed. A monthly check and a check before scaling keep your proof current.

exam.q: Meta approved your betting ad for Nigeria. The brand says it is licensed "in Nigeria". You target Lagos and Abuja. What is the right next step?
options: Launch; approval and a licence are enough
Check which state or federal licence applies to each area you target and get it in writing
Target only Abuja to be safe
Ask the network to run the ads for you
exam.why: Gambling regulation in Nigeria sits largely with states after a 2024 ruling, so a licence must cover the specific places you target. Ad approval is a separate layer.

exam.q: A broker's register entry is authorised, but the domain listed is different from your offer's domain. Your manager says "it is fine, same group". What do you do?
options: Run it; same group is fine
Run at half budget while checking
Pause and get written proof that the offer domain belongs to the licensed entity for your geo
Change your lander to the registered domain
exam.why: A mismatched domain is a clone warning. Only written, verifiable proof clears it, and until then the gate is a no.

exam.q: You plan a crypto exchange campaign in Ghana. The exchange is registered abroad, and you have no platform permission yet. Which gate lines fail?
options: Only the network line
None; crypto is not regulated
Only the copy line
At least the platform line, and the licence line until Ghana coverage is verified
exam.why: At the time of writing many crypto ads need platform permission, and a foreign registration does not prove the exchange may market in Ghana.

exam.q: An iGaming offer allows 18+ in Kenya, but the brand's terms say 21+ for all affiliate traffic. Your CPM is lower at 18 to 24. What age do you set?
options: 21+, because the strictest rule wins
18+, because the law allows it
18+ but exclude interests
25+ to be extra safe and cheaper
exam.why: Leads from 18 to 20 would breach the brand's terms and be rejected. The strictest applicable layer decides.

exam.q: Example: you spent $600 on a forex offer, 12 FTDs at $70 were reported, then the broker found "guaranteed profit" in your ads and withheld everything. What is your result and what would compliant ads at the same cost have earned?
exam.why: Withheld payouts leave you at -$600. At the same cost, 12 x $70 = $840 revenue minus $600 = +$240 profit.

exam.q: A loan costs NGN 6,000 on NGN 40,000 for 30 days. What is the 30-day cost, and what should your ad show as the annual rate?
options: 15%; your own annualised figure
6%; nothing
15%; the lender's official rate as their regulator requires
40%; the total repayable only
exam.why: 6,000 / 40,000 = 15% for 30 days. Official annual rate formulas differ by country, so show the lender's official figure and required example.

exam.q: Your loan lead form collected 200 submissions; 120 ticked the separate partner-sharing box. A buyer offers $4 per lead for all 200. What do you sell?
options: All 200; they filled the form
Only the 120 who consented to sharing
200, but tell the buyer about the 80
None; lead forms cannot be sold
exam.why: Only consented leads can be shared. Selling the other 80 breaches data protection law in many countries and most terms.

exam.q: Your CFD ad's risk warning is in the last line of a long primary text and is cut off on mobile. The ad is approved. What do you do?
options: Nothing; approval means it is fine
Add the warning to the comments
Make the font smaller
Move the warning into the visible text or onto the creative and check each placement
exam.why: Prominence matters. A warning users cannot see without tapping does little, and approval does not prove compliance.

exam.q: Your gambling permission request is pending. The network suggests running the same ads labelled as a "sports news" page meanwhile. What do you do?
options: Decline in writing; it is circumvention, and wait for permission
Run it for 3 days only
Run it on a backup account
Run it with a news lander for reviewers
exam.why: Disguising a restricted category or showing reviewers a different page is circumvention and can get every account involved restricted.

exam.q: Gate check for a new South Africa loans campaign: lender on NCR list (filed), special category declared, network terms filed, copy checked, but consent text has no named recipient. Status?
options: GO; five of six is fine
GO with a smaller budget
NO-GO until the consent text names who gets the data
GO if the lender agrees verbally
exam.why: Any no or unknown line means no launch. Consent must name the recipient before you collect a single lead.
